section_summary: This section contains docket registry sheets and initial documents from State Department decimal file 894.00 covering internal political affairs in Japan from 1934 to 1938. The registry pages catalogue incoming reports on pivotal events, including the February 26, 1936 military coup attempt, the trial and execution of conspirators, the fall of successive cabinets, and foreign policy shifts toward China and the Soviet Union. The included despatches and State Department memoranda analyze the cyclical nature and economic drivers of Japanese expansionism, historical territorial disputes over Saghalien, and the debate over whether liberal or democratic elements under leaders like Koki Hirota could genuinely constrain military dominance.

subfiles.about: A chronological list of papers and docket summary sheet for State Department file 894.00, covering documents from November 1934 through May 1938.
subfiles.summary: This section comprises the State Department's internal registry and docket sheets (pages 42 to 67) listing incoming and outgoing despatches, telegrams, and memoranda concerning Japanese political affairs from late 1934 through May 1938. The entries document major political developments including the February 26, 1936 incident (military coup d'etat and assassinations of key officials), the formation and collapse of successive cabinets under Okada, Hirota, Hayashi, and Konoe, and debates over national mobilization, thought control, and foreign policy toward China and the Soviet Union. Each entry records the document number, date, sender, recipient, and a concise purport of the communication, along with cross-references to other decimal files.
subfiles.title: List of Papers: 894.00 Political Affairs - Japan (Sheets 42-67)

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum analyzing and critiquing Ambassador Grew's despatch regarding the periodicity and economic causes of Japanese expansion.
subfiles.summary: William T. Turner of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs reviews Tokyo Despatch No. 1225, prepared by Erle R. Dickover, which attempted to calculate the probable duration of Japanese expansion based on a theory of periodicity driven by domestic economic pressure and predicted a six to ten year lull following the acquisition of Manchuria. Turner argues that the periodicity thesis is unconvincing because it relies on a very short post-Restoration historical sample and ignores external world conditions. He contends that earlier expansions (such as the Ryukyu, Kurile, and Bonin Islands, and the Sino-Japanese and Russo-Japanese Wars) were primarily motivated by strategic anxieties, Russian expansion, and domestic politics rather than purely economic pressure.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1225: The Rising Tide of Japanese Expansion

subfiles.about: Despatch from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew analyzing historical waves of Japanese expansion and predicting the duration of the current expansionist wave following the seizure of Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew submits a comprehensive historical study (drafted by Erle R. Dickover) analyzing five major waves of Japanese expansion since the Meiji Restoration: 1875-1879 (Ryukyu, Kurile, and Bonin Islands), 1894-1895 (Sino-Japanese War; Formosa, Pescadores, Liaotung), 1904-1905 (Russo-Japanese War; South Manchuria, southern Saghalien), 1914-1922 (World War I, South Seas Mandate, Siberia, Shantung), and 1931-1933 (Manchurian Incident, Shanghai, Jehol). The despatch argues that these waves are fundamentally impelled by domestic economic and population pressure seeking economic opportunity, supported by theories of manifest destiny. Having secured the vast resources of Manchuria and facing growing domestic financial constraints and liberal resistance under Foreign Minister Koki Hirota, Grew suggests the expansionist wave of 1931 has crested and may be followed by a period of six to ten years of quiescence, provided the military does not plunge the nation into catastrophic excesses.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1225: The Rising Tide of Japanese Expansion

subfiles.about: Instruction from the Secretary of State transmitting an English translation of J. O. Levine's historical article on Saghalien in Russo-Japanese relations.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State transmits to the American Embassy in Tokyo a translation of excerpts from an article by J. O. Levine in the July 1935 issue of the French journal Affaires Etrangeres regarding the history of Saghalien (Sakhalin) in Russian and Japanese relations. The article traces the history of the island from early Japanese explorations in 1613 and Dutch navigator Maarten Gerritsz Vries's 1643 voyage, through early Western cartography and eighteenth-century Russian expeditions. It details Japanese official Mogami Tokunai's 1785 expedition, Nikolai Rezanov's rebuffed 1805 mission to Nagasaki and subsequent retaliatory raids by Khvostov and Davydov, and the capture of Russian navigator Vasily Golovnin. The account describes Gennady Nevelskoy's 1849 voyage establishing Saghalien as an island and the Amur as navigable, the establishment of Russian military posts, Russian withdrawal during the Crimean War, and negotiations by Admiral Putyatin leading to the joint occupancy convention of 1867.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 856 to Tokyo: The Island of Saghalien in the Relations between Russia and Japan

subfiles.about: Instruction from the Secretary of State transmitting to the American Embassy in Moscow a translation of J. O. Levine's article on Saghalien.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State transmits to Ambassador William C. Bullitt in Moscow a copy of the translated excerpts from J. O. Levine's article 'The Island of Saghalien in the Relations between Russia and Japan', published in the July 1935 issue of Affaires Etrangeres. The text is provided for the background information of the Ambassador and Embassy staff in Moscow, with an additional copy directed to the American Legation in Riga.
subfiles.title: Instruction to Moscow Transmitting Translation of Article on Saghalien

subfiles.about: Internal State Department memorandum recommending that Under Secretary Phillips read Ambassador Grew's despatch questioning whether democratic forces in Japan are truly strengthening.
subfiles.summary: An officer of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs (initialed EHD/m.m.H.) recommends that Under Secretary of State William Phillips read Tokyo Despatch No. 1255 regarding the alleged strengthening of democratic forces in Japan. The memorandum directs special attention to the concluding paragraph, where Ambassador Grew expresses skepticism toward Foreign Minister Hirota's claims of growing democratic influence. It recalls that the Far Eastern Division has recently queried previous reports from Embassy secretaries asserting a conspicuous growth in Japanese liberal strength.
subfiles.title: Memorandum for Under Secretary Phillips regarding Despatch No. 1255

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting a conversation with Foreign Minister Koki Hirota regarding his belief in the strengthening of democratic forces in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports on a private conversation held with Foreign Minister Koki Hirota following an April 10 dinner for the American Economic Mission. Hirota claimed that his public pledge of 'no war while he is in office' faced no reactionary opposition because it reflected the Emperor's personal views, and asserted that democratic elements in Japan were growing stronger and seeking new political leadership. Hirota noted that while a political party had approached him to assume its leadership, he declined in order to remain non-partisan and avoid factional politics. In conclusion, Grew notes that despite rumors of waning military influence, the Embassy is not yet prepared to endorse Hirota's optimistic view and promises a deeper subsequent analysis.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1255: Alleged Strengthening of the Liberal Element in Japan

subfiles.about: Brief State Department memorandum advising Dr. Hornbeck to reread Tokyo Despatch No. 1279 in light of Koki Hirota's selection as Prime Minister.
subfiles.summary: Cabot Coville (initialed CC) sends a brief routing memorandum to Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck on March 5, 1936, following the February 26 coup attempt in Tokyo. Coville suggests that if Koki Hirota is to become Japan's new Premier, Ambassador Grew's previous Despatch No. 1279 of May 3, 1935, analyzing the liberal element and Hirota's foreign policy methods, is essential reading.
subfiles.title: Memorandum for Dr. Hornbeck regarding Despatch No. 1279 and Hirota as Premier

subfiles.about: Far Eastern Division memorandum evaluating Tokyo Despatch No. 1279 and warning against basing U.S. Far Eastern policy on hopes of Japanese democratization.
subfiles.summary: William T. Turner of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs reviews Ambassador Grew's Despatch No. 1279, concurring with the Embassy's conclusion that despite Foreign Minister Hirota's peaceful and conciliatory rhetoric, the fundamental aggressive goals of Japan have not changed. The memorandum notes that reactionary elements permit Hirota to pursue peaceful diplomacy only so long as it achieves their expansionist objectives without war and at lower cost. It emphasizes that the military retains its preeminence in government and that there is no genuine growth of democratic institutions in the Western sense, advising that the United States should not predicate its Far Eastern policy on expectations of liberal reform in Japan.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1279: Analysis of the Alleged Strengthening of the Liberal Element in Japan

subfiles.about: Detailed despatch by Ambassador Grew examining whether Japanese foreign policy is less inclined toward war, whether the military is losing influence, and whether democratic forces are growing.
subfiles.summary: In amplification of Despatch No. 1255, Ambassador Joseph C. Grew analyzes whether Japan's foreign policy has moderated and whether liberal or democratic elements are genuinely gaining ground. Grew frames his inquiry around three key questions: whether Japanese policy is less inclined toward war, whether the military is losing its dominant influence, and whether democratic strength is expanding. He observes that recent diplomatic developments reflect a distinct trend away from overt belligerence, evidenced by the peaceful conclusion of the Chinese Eastern Railway purchase from the Soviet Union, restrained handling of Barga border incidents, cautious penetration of Chahar, and a press campaign favoring peaceful economic diplomacy in China and moderation toward the United States Navy.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1279: Analysis of the Alleged Strengthening of the Liberal Element in Japan
